column1: Hume — the copy principle: state it, the test it performs, and its one admitted exception.
column2: Principle (Treatise 1.1.1; Enquiry §2): every simple idea is copied from a corresponding simple impression; complex ideas may combine freely, but a term with no impression behind it is empty. Test: challenge any philosophical term to produce its impression. Exception: the missing shade of blue — a simple idea (the unseen shade between two seen ones) seemingly formed without an impression. Hume raises it himself, then dismisses it as "so singular" it is scarcely worth observing. Whether the dismissal is legitimate — a merely interpolative idea vs. a genuine counterexample — is contested.

column1: Hume — the problem of induction: state the dilemma.
column2: (Enquiry §4; Treatise 1.3.6.) All reasoning about matters of fact rests on cause and effect, known only from experience; experience licenses inference to the future only if nature is uniform. Justifying uniformity: demonstratively — impossible, since the contrary (a change in nature's course) is distinctly conceivable without contradiction; or probably, from experience — circular, since probable reasoning itself presupposes the resemblance of past and future. Conclusion: induction has no rational foundation; it is custom, not reason, that carries us. Hume poses the problem; he does not claim to solve it.

column1: Hume — causation: what is missing from constant conjunction, and what supplies it?
column2: (Treatise 1.3.2, 1.3.14; Enquiry §7.) Observing A followed by B repeatedly, we find contiguity, priority, and constant conjunction — never a power or necessary connection in the objects; there is no impression of efficacy. The idea of necessity comes from an impression of reflection: after repetition, the mind is determined by custom to pass from A's impression to B's enlivened idea, and we project that felt determination onto the world. Hence two definitions of cause: the constant conjunction (from the objects) and the mental determination (from the inference). Whether the definitions exhaust Hume's view — skeptical reading — or leave real, unknowable powers standing — the New Hume reading — is disputed.

column1: Hume — liberty and necessity: state the compatibilist case and why the dispute is "merely verbal."
column2: Necessity in matter means uniformity of sequence plus the mind's inference; human actions show the same uniformity (motives → actions, as predictable across history as nature) and inference. Liberty, rightly defined, is the power of acting or not acting according to the will — which everyone possesses — not an absence of necessity; its supposed opposite, chance, does not exist. Since all parties in practice acknowledge both, the dispute is merely verbal: it persisted because the terms were never defined. Objection (van Inwagen's consequence argument): if acts are necessitated by a past we do not control, they are not up to us — a challenge the verbal-dissolution reply must still meet.

column1: Hume — "Of Miracles": state the maxim and the modern dispute about what it proves.
column2: (Enquiry §10.) A miracle is a violation of a law of nature, a law resting on firm and unalterable experience; testimony is believed only from experience of its reliability. So proof stands against proof, and "a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence" (§10.4): no testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact attested — and even then the stronger proof wins only by the excess. Applied (Part II): no miracle meets the standard. Dispute: Earman reads the maxim as an a priori bar no evidence could pass (a Bayesian error about priors); Fogelin defends it as an evidential-weighing rule. Presented as a dispute, not settled.

column1: Hume — Philo on design: the three presses on the analogy.
column2: (Dialogues, Parts II, V; Philo's speeches, not narration — speaker attribution is disputed.) (1) Weak analogy: the universe resembles a machine only remotely — as much a vegetable or animal (generation, vegetation) — and analogy weakens as resemblance thins. (2) Unique case: we infer a house's architect from having seen houses built; of universe-making we have seen none, so cause-and-effect reasoning forbids the inference. (3) Proportionality: even granted, it licenses no attributes beyond what it requires — not infinity, perfection, or unity (a committee of gods, an infant or superannuated deity, fit as well). Part XII's concession — a cause bearing "some remote analogy" to intelligence — keeps the operative word: remote.

column1: Hume — the problem of evil in the Dialogues: the old questions and the four hypotheses.
column2: (Dialogues, Parts X–XI.) Philo revives "Epicurus's old questions" — attributed by Philo to Epicurus, not Hume's coinage: Is God willing to prevent evil but unable? Then he is not omnipotent. Able but unwilling? Then malevolent. Both able and willing? Whence, then, is evil? Part XI runs four hypotheses about the first cause's moral character: perfectly good, perfectly evil, mixed, or neither. The phenomena — good and evil indifferently mixed, no distribution by desert — fit neither best: a morally indifferent cause. The argument targets the inference to God's moral attributes from nature, not bare existence; the free-will and soul-making replies are the literature's, not Hume's, labeled as such in the dossier.

column1: Hume — the bundle theory of the self, and the Appendix's confession.
column2: Introspection finds no impression of a simple, identical self — only particular perceptions: "I never can catch myself at any time without a perception" (Treatise 1.4.6). The mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity" — a theater with no stage. Identity is ascribed, not perceived, manufactured by resemblance and causation among perceptions. The Appendix confession: his two principles — all perceptions are distinct existences; the mind never perceives any real connection among them — he "cannot render consistent; nor is it possible for me to renounce either of them." Hume offers no repair; Garrett (reconciliation) and Parfit (reductionism embraced) are its continuations.

column1: Hume — "Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions": state the argument, not the slogan.
column2: (Treatise 2.3.3.) Reason has two offices: demonstrating relations of ideas, and inferring matters of fact. Neither can motivate: abstract relations move no one, and factual beliefs move us only through desires they serve (fruit moves us through appetite). A passion is an "original existence," not a copy of anything, so it cannot be true or false — and only what can be true or false can be contrary to reason. Hence reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will; only a contrary passion can. The slogan is the conclusion. Objection (Nagel, McDowell): reasons can themselves motivate; reply (Michael Smith): belief/desire direction of fit — the dispute continues.

column1: Hume — is–ought: what the paragraph says, and the three readings.
column2: (Treatise 3.1.1.27.) Authors proceed with is/is not and then, imperceptibly, reason with ought/ought not — "a new relation or affirmation" needing to be observed and explained, since it seems "altogether inconceivable" how it could be deduced from the others. Three readings: (1) the categorical "Hume's Law" — no normative conclusion from purely factual premises; (2) the narrower reading — a demand, inside the anti-rationalist campaign, that moral distinctions cannot be deduced by reason alone; (3) MacIntyre's challenge — a casualty report on a broken tradition, not a logical law. Searle's institutional-facts counterexample (promising) tests reading (1); rejoinder: the premise smuggles in the norm. The dossier presents the dispute unsettled.

column1: Hume — moral distinctions: not from reason; sympathy and the general point of view.
column2: Reason judges truth and falsehood; morality influences action, which reason cannot do; so vice and virtue are perceived by sentiment, as sounds and colors are — the oak that drops a sapling is a parricide in relations, innocent, showing relations alone carry no morals (Treatise 3.1.1–2; EPM 5, 9, App. 1). Raw sympathy is partial (stronger for the near and dear). Correction: we survey character from a general point of view — the standpoint of those affected, taken steadily and in common — stabilizing moral judgment and making shared moral language possible. The EPM recasts the machinery: sympathy broadens into humanity; qualities approved as useful or agreeable, to self or others.

column1: Hume — justice as an artificial virtue: convention without contract, and the sensible knave.
column2: Circumstances: moderate scarcity plus limited generosity make possessions unstable. Remedy (Treatise 3.2.2; EPM 3, App. 3): a convention — a general sense of common interest, mutually expressed — like two men rowing a boat: coordinated action with no promise, promises being possible only once conventions exist (so contract cannot found it). Justice is artificial: its rules (stability of possession, transfer by consent, promises) are devices, founded in nature's needs. Hume's test, the sensible knave (EPM 9): he keeps the rules generally but breaks them whenever a secret violation pays. Hume's answer — the knave trades "the invaluable enjoyment of a character" for a lesser gain — a partial concession, not a refutation.

column1: Hume — mitigated skepticism: what it permits, what it forbids, and the role of backgammon.
column2: Pyrrhonian doubt, pushed to the limit (Treatise 1.4.1–7), refutes itself in practice: it produces melancholy, and nature cures it — "I dine, I play a game of back-gammon, I converse" — not by answering the arguments but by removing their hold; the philosopher returns to philosophy on nature's terms, governed by sentiment. Mitigated (Academical) skepticism (Enquiry §12) keeps the lesson: modesty about our faculties, inquiry confined to abstract reasoning and matters of fact proportioned to them, belief apportioned to evidence. Whether the resting point is stable (Kemp Smith's naturalism: belief as an act of the sensitive, not the cogitative, part) or skepticism outlasted (Reid, Stroud) is the standing dispute — left open.

column1: Hume — impressions and ideas: the distinction and its two kinds of each.
column2: Concepts (Treatise 1.1.1; Enquiry §2). All perceptions divide by force and vivacity: impressions — sensations, passions, emotions, felt with full vivacity; ideas — their fainter copies in thinking and reasoning. Impressions divide into sensation (from the senses; their ultimate causes are, Hume says, inexplicable by human reason) and reflection (from ideas — desires, volitions, feelings occasioned by ideas of pleasure or pain). Ideas divide into simple (admitting no separation) and complex (built by imagination from simples — the golden mountain, the virtuous horse). The distinction is the engine room: the copy principle, the meaning test, and the account of belief (an idea enlivened toward an impression's force) all run on it.

column1: Hume — Hume's fork: the two kinds of objects of human reason, and its later name.
column2: (Enquiry §4.1; "Hume's fork" is a later label — Hume never uses the phrase.) Relations of ideas: demonstrable, known independent of experience (arithmetic, geometry); their denial implies contradiction. Matters of fact: contingent, known only from experience; their contraries are possible. All objects fall under one prong. The fork frames the induction problem (matters of fact cannot be promoted to relations of ideas) and supplies the Enquiry's closing test: a volume containing neither abstract reasoning nor experimental reasoning about fact goes "to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion" (§12). Pressure point: which side of the fork the copy principle falls on is a standing exam question.

column1: Hume — association of ideas: the three principles and what they explain.
column2: Ideas connect by three principles (Treatise 1.1.4; Enquiry §3): resemblance, contiguity in time or place, and cause and effect — "a gentle force" of attraction in the mental world, as regular as gravity in Newton's. Association is the mind's grammar: it explains the transitions of thought and imagination, complex ideas, and — through cause and effect's dominance over the others — why belief and causal inference feel compelled. In the Treatise it also underwrites the ascribed identity of objects and selves (resemblance and causation among perceptions smoothing succession into "identity"). Hume claims the discovery modestly and uses it immodestly: it is the cement his science of man is mortared with.

column1: Hume — custom (habit): Hume's skeptical solution to his skeptical problem.
column2: Custom is "the great guide of human life" (Enquiry §5): the propensity, produced by repetition, to expect the same events from similar objects — operating before reasoning, in children and animals, irresistible in philosophers at dinner. Hume's answer-form to induction: not a justification (none exists) but an explanation — nature, by custom, determines us to judge of the future by the past, an instinct as constitutional as feeling heat or cold. Distinguish: custom explains belief's origin; it does not confer the warrant the problem showed to be missing. That gap — explanation without justification — is either the system's honesty or its quiet scandal, depending on the reading.

column1: Hume — belief: an idea with a manner, not an extra idea.
column2: Concept (Treatise 1.3.7; Enquiry §5.2). What distinguishes believing "Caesar died in his bed" from merely conceiving it? Not content — the ideas are the same — but manner: belief is a lively, forceful, steady conception, an idea raised toward the vivacity of an impression by its customary connection with a present impression. Belief is "more properly an act of the sensitive, than of the cogitative part of our natures" (T 1.4.1). Consequences: belief admits of degrees set by experience's frequency and freshness (the probability sections); it cannot be willed directly; and assent in philosophy and in common life is one mechanism, not two — the premise of the whole mitigated-skeptical settlement.

column1: Hume — sympathy in the Treatise vs. the Principles of Morals.
column2: Concept (Treatise 2.1.11, 3.3.1; EPM 5). Treatise machinery: sympathy is a conversion mechanism — from another's outward signs I form an idea of their passion; the idea, enlivened by resemblance, contiguity, and the ever-present impression of my own self, crosses into an impression: I come to feel it. It explains pride's sociality, esteem for the rich, and moral approval's reach beyond self-interest. In the EPM the apparatus is replaced: sympathy survives as a principle of humanity or fellow-feeling, doing its work without the conversion machinery. Textbooks that export the Treatise's mechanism into the EPM (or vice versa) misread both; the dossier keeps the shift visible as evidence of Hume's revising.

column1: Hume — artificial vs. natural virtues.
column2: Concept (Treatise 3.2.1; EPM App./§§3–4 framing). Natural virtues — benevolence, generosity, parental affection — approve directly from instinct or immediate sentiment, act by act, whether or not any system exists. Artificial virtues — justice, fidelity to promises, allegiance, chastity in Hume's list — require a convention: a single act of justice may even harm the public; the whole scheme, universally practiced, is what approval attaches to. The distinction is not praise-ranking (artificial does not mean fake or lesser — justice is indispensable, benevolence merely lovely) but architecture: which virtues need society's scaffolding and which precede it. The sensible-knave problem and the rowing-boat convention belong to the artificial side.

column1: Hume — the science of man: the Treatise's master project.
column2: Concept (Treatise, Introduction). The experimental method of Newton — experience and observation, hypotheses framed cautiously from phenomena — applied to moral subjects: "the science of man is the only solid foundation for the other sciences," since logic, morals, criticism, and politics all study the principles of human nature. One system explains knowing, feeling, and valuing: principles of association govern ideas; custom governs inference; sympathy governs morals. The ambition explains the Treatise's scale and its collapse-risk: when the central principles (selfhood, causation's necessity) turn out thinner than the system needs, the Appendix's confession follows. Kant, Reid, and the positivists each inherit a different fragment of the project.

column1: Hume — the New Hume debate: what is actually being fought over.
column2: Dispute (reception; dossier 06). Question: did Hume deny that causation involves real, objective necessary connections in nature — or only that we can know or conceive them? Skeptical (regularity) reading: the two definitions exhaust his considered view; necessity is the mind's projection. New Hume (Wright 1983; Galen Strawson 1989; Buckle): Hume was a causal realist — he believed in powers and secrets of nature, skeptical only about our access; the skeptical reading mistakes an epistemological limit for a metaphysical denial. Middle positions (Beebee: epistemology first, metaphysics deliberately uncommitted) complicate the binary. The dossier presents the dispute with its evidence (texts each side quotes) and settles nothing.

column1: Hume — skeptic vs. naturalist: the master dispute over the whole philosophy.
column2: Dispute (reception; dossier 06). Kemp Smith (1905 articles; The Philosophy of David Hume, 1941): Hume is a naturalist — the point of the skeptical arguments is to subordinate reason to instinct and feeling; belief, sympathy, and morals are nature's work, and the skepticism is the instrument. Skeptical readings (Fogelin; in part Stroud, Hume, 1977): the negative arguments retain full force and priority; the naturalism explains why we cannot help believing, without restoring what the arguments destroyed. The choice between them reorganizes everything downstream — the induction problem's sting, the backgammon passage's meaning (position vs. surrender), and the Dialogues' residue. The dossier flags each fork where the readings diverge, and takes no side.

column1: Hume — the 1777 Advertisement: the author's verdict the dossier reports but does not obey.
column2: Framing (Treatise posthumous editions, Advertisement dated 1777). Hume, correcting proofs for the posthumous edition, directs readers "that the following Pieces [the two Enquiries and the shorter works] may alone be regarded as containing his philosophical sentiments and principles" — disowning the Treatise as a juvenile work, marred by "negligence of composition." Facts to hold together: he kept profiting from the Treatise's contents in the recastings; the disowning also served the Treatise's attackers (a young man's indiscretion, officially past). Scholarly practice reads both — the Enquiries for Hume's presentation, the Treatise for the fuller system — and this dossier follows the Advertisement's order (Enquiries first) while declining its verdict, with the counter-position stated.

column1: Hume — impressions of reflection: how the passions enter the system.
column2: Concept (Treatise 1.1.2, Book II passim). Reflection impressions: calm and violent feelings arising from ideas — desire and aversion, hope and fear, pride and humility, love and hatred — as distinct from sensation impressions (hot, cold, colored) arriving unbidden. Their causal place: an idea of pleasure or pain (copied from a sensation impression) occasions the reflective impression, becoming the will's spring. Book II's double relation of impressions and ideas (pride: the pleasant impression of a quality, the idea of self as its object) runs on this category — and the slave-of-the-passions argument presupposes it: passions are original existences because they are impressions, not copies of anything that could be false.

column1: Hume — the sensible knave: Hume's hardest test of his own moral theory.
column2: (EPM 9.2.) The knave accepts the general rule — honesty is the best policy — and keeps it, but breaks it whenever a secret violation promises advantage without endangering the social union: utility alone seems to license him, since the single breach harms no one and enriches him. Hume's reply is not more utility but character: the knave forfeits “the invaluable enjoyment of a character” and the inward peace of self-approval. Hume records the case as a partial concession, not a refutation: in the exceptional instance his theory has no answer the knave must accept.

column1: Hume — constant conjunction: the observable whole of causation.
column2: Concept (Treatise 1.3.2; Enquiry §7). Strip a causal sequence to what is perceivable: the cause is contiguous, prior, and — across all resembling instances — constantly conjoined with the effect. Nothing more is in the objects: no glue, power, or tie meets eye or instrument. This austerity is the premise of the entire causation file: the two definitions (Argument 3), the projection account of necessity, and the induction problem (constant conjunctions of the past are all experience ever shows). Caveat for the New Hume dispute: "nothing more is perceived" is agreed by all sides; whether "nothing more exists" follows is precisely the fight.

column1: Hume — the general point of view: sympathy's correction, and morals' shared standpoint.
column2: Concept (Treatise 3.3.1; EPM 9). Left to itself, sympathy varies with distance, relation, and presence; moral judgments would collide. So we take up a "steady and general" point of view: we survey character in relation to those who have commerce with its possessor, discount our own position, using a common vocabulary of praise and blame from that standpoint — much as we correct visual judgments for distance. The mechanism makes moral objectivity-without-reason possible in Hume: not a perception of moral facts, but a disciplined sentiment. Its EPM descendant is the sentiment of humanity, corrected by "a general view" — continuity across the recasting is real; the machinery differs.

column1: Hume — convention: coordination with neither promise nor sovereign.
column2: Concept (Treatise 3.2.2). A convention arises when each person perceives the others' sense of common interest and regulates conduct on the expectation of reciprocity — "the actions of each of us have a reference to those of the other." Hume's figure: two men rowing a boat pull together by convention though they have never given promises to each other. The category matters because it breaks the contractarian fork (either explicit contract or mere force): language, money, weights and measures, and justice itself are conventions — self-sustaining once running, no legislator required at the origin. Rousseau's and later game theory's interest in Hume starts here.

column1: Hume — "Of the Standard of Taste": the general point of view, exported to aesthetics.
column2: Concept (Essays, 1757). Beauty is no quality in things themselves; it exists in the sentiment of the beholder. Yet not all sentiments are equal: the standard of taste is the joint verdict of true judges — "strong sense, united to delicate sentiment, improved by practice, perfected by comparison, and cleared of all prejudice" — whose delicacy of imagination, practice, and freedom from prejudice are themselves empirically testable marks (Sancho's kinsmen and the leather-and-iron key). Blameless diversity remains (age, temperament, national manners), which Hume treats as a boundary on the standard, not a defeat of it. The file tests whether the Week 3 machinery of corrected sentiment travels from morals to art.

column1: Hume — who speaks in the Dialogues? The distribution problem.
column2: Dispute (Dialogues; dossier 06). The dialogue gives Philo the strongest arguments, Demea the exits, Cleanthes the position Hume's contemporaries expected him to attack — and Pamphilus's sentence awards the palm to Cleanthes. Kemp Smith's thesis (introduction to his 1935 edition): Philo is Hume's spokesman and the verdict is protective irony. Counter-readings: Hume's views distribute across speakers (Cleanthes's experiential theism, Philo's skepticism, and Part XII's thin concession each holding a piece); some take Pamphilus straight. Evidence discipline: the manuscript history (drafted by 1751, revised to the eve of death, published posthumously 1779) explains caution without identifying a voice. The dossier assigns no spokesman; study question and audit both treat the distribution as open.
